question: Where do I find a fractional CRO in Ann Arbor?
body:
## Direct Answer

You find a fractional CRO in Ann Arbor through three main channels: specialized fractional-executive networks (Chief Outsiders, Bolster, Go Fractional, Continuum), the University of Michigan and Ann Arbor SPARK entrepreneurial ecosystem, and local RevOps and go-to-market advisors who already operate in the region's SaaS, medtech, and mobility corridors. The most reliable path is to run several of these channels at once rather than betting on one: post the role to a national fractional network for pre-screened breadth, ask Ann Arbor SPARK's mentor and investor programs for warm introductions, tap your board and portfolio-company network, and run a targeted LinkedIn search on "fractional CRO," "fractional VP Sales," and "revenue advisor" filtered to the Detroit–Ann Arbor metro. Before you contact anyone, define the revenue problem you are actually solving in one sentence, then match it to an operator who has personally run that exact motion — a founder-led SaaS company crossing $2M ARR needs a very different operator than a medtech firm building its first enterprise sales team. Vet on pattern match, evidence, and references; scope a 30- and 90-day plan with explicit metrics before signing; and decide honestly whether you need a hands-on player-coach who is in the room weekly or a strategy-and-systems operator who can work mostly remote. Do that, and a metro the size of Ann Arbor gives you a deeper bench of qualified part-time revenue leaders than its population would suggest.

Ann Arbor is an unusually rich hunting ground for a fractional Chief Revenue Officer because it sits at the intersection of a top research university, a dense venture-backed startup scene anchored by Ann Arbor SPARK, and mature enterprises in mobility, life sciences, and enterprise software. That means the pool of experienced revenue leaders willing to work part-time — one to three days a week, for a fraction of a full-time compensation package — is deeper here than in most metros of comparable size. The trick is knowing where those operators cluster, how to vet them so you get a builder rather than a figurehead, and how to structure the engagement so it produces durable revenue infrastructure instead of an expensive slide deck.

## What exactly is a fractional CRO, and when does an Ann Arbor company need one?

A fractional CRO is a senior revenue executive who takes ownership of your entire go-to-market engine — sales, marketing alignment, customer success, pricing, and revenue operations — but on a part-time or contract basis rather than as a full-time hire. Unlike a consultant who delivers recommendations and leaves, a fractional CRO carries a leadership mandate: they own the number, build and manage the team, install the operating cadence, and stay accountable for pipeline and net revenue outcomes over a defined engagement, typically three to twelve months. The word that separates the role from advisory work is *accountability*. A consultant is measured on the quality of their advice; a fractional CRO is measured on whether the pipeline grew and the forecast started coming true.

The Ann Arbor companies that get the most value from this model share a profile. They are usually post–product-market-fit but pre–Series B: annual recurring revenue somewhere between roughly one and fifteen million dollars, a founder or first sales hire who has stopped scaling, and a board or investor pushing for repeatable, forecastable growth. A founder-led SaaS company spun out of University of Michigan research, a medtech firm graduating from grant funding to commercial sales, or a mobility supplier trying to build an enterprise sales motion into automotive OEMs are all textbook cases. When the revenue problem is *systemic* — no defined sales stages, unreliable forecasting, marketing and sales pointing fingers, a founder who is still the only person who can close — a fractional CRO fixes the machine. When the problem is simply "we need more reps dialing," you want a sales manager or another account executive, not a CRO. Diagnosing that difference correctly is the single most important step, because hiring a strategic revenue leader to solve a capacity problem wastes senior-operator money, and hiring a rep to solve a systems problem leaves the machine broken.

A useful gut check: write down the specific outcome you expect in ninety days. If the answer is "a working forecast, defined sales stages, a comp plan that aligns behavior, and two hired-and-ramped reps," that is a fractional CRO mandate. If the answer is "forty more discovery calls a week," that is a capacity hire. The clearer you are on that distinction before outreach, the faster and cheaper your search becomes.

## Where do I actually find candidates in and around Ann Arbor?

There are five practical channels, and the best searches use several in parallel rather than betting on one. The first is the **fractional-executive networks** that vet and place these operators nationally but staff regionally. Chief Outsiders, Bolster, Go Fractional, and Continuum all maintain rosters of revenue leaders, many of whom live in or will travel to the Detroit–Ann Arbor corridor. These networks pre-screen for the operating experience most founders can't assess on their own, which shortens your vetting cycle considerably and gives you a fallback if your first candidate isn't the right fit.

The second channel is the **Ann Arbor and Southeast Michigan startup ecosystem itself.** Ann Arbor SPARK — the region's economic development and entrepreneurial support organization — runs mentor-in-residence programs, an entrepreneur boot camp, and an investor network, and its staff can often make warm introductions to revenue operators who have exited or advise locally. The University of Michigan's Zell Lurie Institute at the Ross School of Business and the Center for Entrepreneurship in the College of Engineering both maintain alumni and mentor networks heavy with commercial leadership talent. These are not staffing agencies, so treat them as referral channels rather than marketplaces — but a warm introduction from a program director who knows both parties is worth ten cold applications.

The third channel is **local RevOps and go-to-market advisory firms and independent operators** who already work with Michigan-based companies. Many market themselves as fractional revenue leaders even when they don't use that exact title — you'll see "revenue advisor," "GTM operator," or "fractional VP Sales." The fourth is **your investor and board network.** Michigan-based funds and the broader Detroit-area venture community run portfolio-wide talent networks and frequently share fractional operators across companies; a single introduction from a portfolio partner can surface someone who has already been vetted by a company you trust. The fifth is **LinkedIn and warm referral**, which remains, unglamorously, the highest-hit-rate channel of all when you search by location plus "fractional CRO," "fractional VP Sales," or "revenue advisor," then ask your network for a warm path to the two or three names that look strongest.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Define the revenue problem] --> B{Systemic or tactical}
  B -->|Systemic| C[Fractional CRO search]
  B -->|Tactical| D[Sales manager or rep]
  C --> E[Fractional networks]
  C --> F[Ann Arbor SPARK and U-M]
  C --> G[Investor and board referrals]
  C --> H[LinkedIn regional search]
  E --> I[Shortlist three to five]
  F --> I
  G --> I
  H --> I
  I --> J[Structured vetting]
  J --> K[Scoped engagement]
```

Run at least three of these channels at once. A national network gives you breadth and pre-screening; the local ecosystem gives you operators who understand Michigan's talent market, sales cycles, and the specific rhythms of selling into automotive suppliers, health systems, and university procurement. The overlap between those two lists — a nationally vetted operator with real regional context — is your strongest shortlist, and it is worth waiting a week or two to find that overlap rather than signing the first available name.

## How do I vet a fractional CRO so I get a builder, not a figurehead?

Vetting a fractional revenue leader is different from vetting a full-time hire because you have less time and the engagement is inherently lower-commitment on both sides. Concentrate your diligence on three things: **pattern match, evidence, and references.**

Pattern match means the candidate has personally run the specific motion you need. If you sell six-figure enterprise deals with nine-month cycles and multiple stakeholders, an operator whose entire career was product-led self-serve growth is a mismatch no matter how impressive the logo history — the playbooks barely overlap. Ask them to walk you through a real deal or a real quarter, not a philosophy. The good ones get concrete fast: they talk about pipeline coverage ratios, stage conversion, ramp time, discount discipline, and the exact levers they pulled to move the number. Vague answers about "building a high-performing culture" without mechanics are a warning sign.

Evidence means asking for artifacts and outcomes. A real operator can describe the forecasting cadence they installed, the compensation plan they redesigned and why, the pipeline they built from what starting point to what ending point, and how long it took. Be alert for the figurehead pattern — someone who name-drops strategy but goes vague the moment you ask "how, specifically, and what happened next?" References are the final gate: talk to at least two founders or CEOs the candidate has actually served in a fractional capacity, and ask the disqualifying question directly — *would you hire them again, and what did they get wrong?* The willingness to answer that second half candidly, from both the candidate and their references, tells you more than any polished pitch.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Candidate intro] --> B[Pattern match check]
  B --> C[Evidence and artifacts]
  C --> D[Two founder references]
  D --> E{Would you rehire them}
  E -->|Yes| F[Scope thirty day plan]
  E -->|No| G[Pass]
  F --> H[Define success metrics]
  H --> I[Signed engagement]
```

Structure the whole process against a defined scorecard so you're comparing candidates on the same axes — motion match, systems experience, hiring track record, references, presence cadence — rather than on charisma. One filter matters specifically in a market like Ann Arbor: ask whether they will actually be *in the room.* Some of the best fractional operators are stretched across five clients simultaneously. For a company that needs hands-on team-building, a leader who can spend one full day a week on-site — or at minimum in the same time zone and available for live pipeline reviews — beats a bigger name who only surfaces on a monthly video call. Ask directly how many other clients they carry and which day of the week is yours.

## What should a fractional CRO engagement cost, and how is it structured?

Pricing for fractional revenue leadership varies with scope, seniority, and time commitment, and you should be skeptical of any quote that arrives before scope is defined. Engagements are typically structured one of three ways: a **monthly retainer** for a fixed number of days per month; a **project or milestone fee** for a defined build (for example, "install a forecasting system and hire two account executives in ninety days"); or a **retainer plus performance component** tied to pipeline or revenue milestones. What you should insist on is not a specific dollar figure — which depends entirely on your stage and needs — but *clarity*: how many days per week or month, which outcomes, what cadence of reporting, and a clean exit or conversion clause.

The structural decisions matter more than the headline rate. Define a thirty-day plan and a ninety-day plan before signing, each with explicit success metrics — pipeline coverage ratio, forecast accuracy, stage conversion, ramp milestones, a hired-and-onboarded rep count. Agree on how the fractional CRO's authority interacts with your existing team so reps know who they report to and who owns hiring decisions; ambiguity here is where these engagements quietly fail. And build in a conversion path. Many of the best fractional engagements are effectively auditions for a full-time hire, or a bridge until you can afford one, so it is worth agreeing early on what a transition to permanent — or a clean wind-down — looks like. Founders who skip this step often end up paying senior-operator rates for advice they can't operationalize, which is the most common way these engagements disappoint. Put the presence cadence and the metrics in writing, because "available as needed" is the phrase under which fractional relationships slowly decay.

## Does the fractional CRO need to be physically in Ann Arbor?

Not necessarily — and being rigid about geography can cost you the best candidate. The normalization of remote and hybrid work has widened the fractional talent pool dramatically, and many companies successfully run a fractional CRO who lives in Chicago, Boston, or Austin and travels in for key weeks. What matters far more than a local zip code is *time-zone alignment, market familiarity, and cadence of presence.* An operator in the Eastern or Central time zone who understands how to sell into automotive suppliers, health systems, or research institutions will serve an Ann Arbor company better than a local generalist who has never run your motion.

That said, physical proximity has real, underrated advantages for early-stage team-building. If your fractional CRO needs to sit next to a first sales hire, run live pipeline reviews, coach on real calls, and read the room during a founder-to-sales handoff, someone who can be on-site in Ann Arbor one day a week creates compounding value a fully remote arrangement can't match. The practical resolution is to weigh the *specific work* the role demands: a systems-and-strategy build tolerates remote well; a hands-on player-coach hiring and ramping a team benefits from local presence. Decide which kind of engagement you actually need before you let geography narrow — or over-narrow — your list, and regardless of where the operator sits, insist on a fixed, predictable presence cadence written into the contract.

## FAQ

### What's the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?

A fractional CRO owns the revenue number and builds the team and systems under a leadership mandate; a consultant advises and delivers recommendations but carries no ongoing accountability for pipeline or hires. Choose the CRO when you need someone accountable for outcomes and empowered to make people and process decisions, not just to produce a plan you then have to execute yourself.

### How quickly can I get a fractional CRO started?

Faster than a full-time hire — often within two to four weeks. Fractional networks pre-screen candidates, and because the commitment is lower-risk for both sides, the decision cycle compresses. The gating factor is usually your own clarity on scope, not candidate availability, so time spent defining the mandate up front pays back directly in a faster start.

### What size company is a fractional CRO right for?

Typically companies with roughly one to fifteen million in ARR that are post–product-market-fit but not yet able or ready to fund a full-time CRO. Below that range, a fractional VP of Sales or a revenue advisor usually fits better; well above it, you likely need a permanent revenue leader. Match the role to the stage of your revenue problem, not to a vanity title.

### Do fractional CROs work with non-software companies?

Yes. Ann Arbor's medtech, mobility, advanced manufacturing, and professional-services firms all use fractional revenue leaders. The key is matching the operator to your specific sales motion — enterprise, channel, or transactional — rather than assuming the role is SaaS-only. A leader who has run long, multi-stakeholder industrial deals is a poor fit for high-velocity transactional sales, and vice versa.

### How is a fractional CRO different from an interim CRO?

An interim CRO is a full-time placeholder filling a vacant seat until a permanent hire is made, usually working five days a week for a short, defined period. A fractional CRO is an ongoing part-time arrangement, working a defined slice of the week on a recurring basis. Interim is about covering a gap; fractional is about buying senior leadership you don't yet need full-time.

### Should a seed-stage startup hire a fractional CRO?

Usually not a full CRO. At seed stage, a fractional VP of Sales or a revenue advisor is a better fit, because the problem is typically finding a repeatable motion rather than scaling one. A CRO becomes valuable once you have early traction and a systemic go-to-market problem to solve — unreliable forecasting, no defined process, marketing and sales misalignment — not just a need for more selling activity.

### How do I know if the engagement is working?

Track leading indicators from day one: pipeline coverage ratio, forecast accuracy, sales-stage conversion, ramp time for new hires, and whether the team is actually adopting the process the CRO installed. Meaningful movement should appear within the first sixty to ninety days. If the only outputs after two months are documents and meetings, raise it directly — a fractional CRO should be changing what happens in the pipeline, not just describing it.

### What's the biggest mistake companies make when hiring one?

Hiring for a résumé instead of a motion match, and failing to define success metrics up front. A leader with an impressive logo history but no experience running your specific sales cycle will underperform a lesser-known operator who has run exactly your motion. The second most common mistake is leaving authority ambiguous, so the fractional CRO can advise but can't actually make the hiring and process decisions the mandate requires.
